title: De eximio usu methodi interpolationum in serierum doctrina

deep.reconstruction:
Problem 3 (§30) asks for a curve y(x) that takes prescribed values p, q, r, s, … at the equally spaced abscissas x = nθ, (n+1)θ, (n+2)θ, …. This is interpolation on a one-sided infinite lattice.

Euler sets x = θω. He applies his general infinite-product Lagrange formula of §10 with the nodes ±(n+k). The interpolant is therefore odd in ω: y/ω is a sum of terms even in ω, with value y_k at ω = n+k.

In modern form the cardinal function for node n+k is
L_k(ω) = (ω/(n+k)) ∏_{j≠k} ((n+j)^2 − ω^2)/((n+j)^2 − (n+k)^2).

The coefficient 𝔄 of p is the infinite product
∏_{k≥1} (n+k−ω)(n+k+ω)/(k(2n+k)).
This is of the type ∏ (a+k−1)(c+k−1)/((b+k−1)(d+k−1)) with a = n+1−ω, b = 1, c = n+1+ω, d = 2n+1 and a+c = b+d. Euler evaluates it via his product-to-integral formula of §17. In modern terms
𝔄 = Γ(2n+1)/(Γ(n+1−ω)Γ(n+1+ω)).

The ratios 𝔅/𝔄 = 2(n+1)(n²−ω²)/((n+1)²−ω²), etc., follow by telescoping. They give 𝔅, ℭ, 𝔇, … as rational multiples of 𝔄. These are correct, e.g. ℭ = (n+2)(2n+1)(n²−ω²)/((n+2)²−ω²)·𝔄.

The final interpolation formula has the shape
N(ω)·y = Σ_k (−1)^k [(2n)_k/k!] y_k/((n+k)²−ω²),
with (2n)_k = 2n(2n+1)…(2n+k−1). Here N(ω) is a Gamma-type normaliser that Euler writes as nΔ/(2(n+ω)ω). This is a Gamma-weighted cardinal (Whittaker-type) series, equivalently a Mittag-Leffler partial-fraction expansion of y/G, where G = 1/(Γ(n−ω)Γ(n+ω)).

Modern check of the normaliser. Correctly,
y = [ω(n+ω)/(n·B(n−ω, n+ω+1))]·Σ_k (−1)^k [(2n)_k/k!] y_k/((n+k)²−ω²).
So the correct statement is 𝔄 = 1/((n−ω)B(n−ω, n+ω+1)), and Euler's Δ ought to be 2∫₀¹ z^{n−ω−1}(1−z)^{n+ω} dz.

Euler instead obtains 𝔄 = 1/((n−ω)∫ z^{n−ω}(1−z)^{n−ω−1} dz) = 2/((n−ω)B(n−ω, n−ω)). The step from one-half to the symmetric Beta integral is itself correct, since B(a+1, a) = B(a, a)/2. However, the resulting expression depends only on n−ω. It agrees with the true value only at ω = 0.

On the next page he uses n = 1/2, θ = π, where the series becomes Σ 4/((2k+1)² − 4ω²) = (π/2ω) tan πω. From this he concludes Δ = (1+2ω)π/cos ωπ. That value is exactly 2B(1/2−ω, 3/2+ω), i.e. the correct normaliser. It is NOT B(1/2−ω, 1/2−ω): at ω = 1/4 the latter is Γ(1/4)²/√π ≈ 7.42, whereas 1.5π/cos(π/4) ≈ 6.66.

Thus the page's Δ-integral is wrong, and the following page's 'evaluation' of Δ is a false identity.
errors:
The integral representation of 𝔄 (hence of Δ) is wrong.
- Printed: 𝔄 = 1/((n−ω)∫z^{n−ω}(1−z)^{n−ω−1}dz), i.e. Δ = B(n−ω, n−ω).
- Correct: 𝔄 = Γ(2n+1)/(Γ(n+1−ω)Γ(n+1+ω)) = 1/((n−ω)B(n−ω, n+1+ω)), so Euler's Δ should be 2B(n−ω, n+ω+1) = 2∫z^{n−ω−1}(1−z)^{n+ω}dz.
- The two agree only at ω = 0. Likely cause: a misapplication of the §17 product–integral formula, with the c = n+1+ω factor effectively replaced by one depending on n−ω.

Consequence on the next page: the claimed identity ∫z^{−ω−1/2}(1−z)^{−ω−1/2}dz = (1+2ω)π/cos ωπ is false (ω = 1/4: 7.42 vs 6.66). The right-hand side is the correct value of the corrected Δ, 2B(1/2−ω, 3/2+ω).

Euler's subsequent Scholion attributes possible failure to the non-uniqueness of the interpolating curve. For n = 1/2, θ = π, however, the cardinal series reproduces sin exactly. The real defect is the normalising integral.

ideas.what: Lagrange interpolation through infinitely many equally spaced nodes ±(n+k), with an infinite-product cardinal function and Gamma-normalised partial-fraction series y ∝ Σ(−1)^k binom(2n+k−1,k) y_k/((n+k)²−ω²)
ideas.modern_name: Cardinal/Lagrange interpolation series on a lattice (Gamma-weighted Whittaker cardinal series; Mittag-Leffler expansion)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lagrange/Euler for finite cases; infinite cardinal series to E. T. Whittaker (1915), Nörlund for Gamma-weighted forms
ideas.where_published: E555 itself (Opuscula Analytica I, 1783), building on §10 of the same paper

ideas.what: Evaluating infinite products ∏(a+k)(c+k)/((b+k)(d+k)) with a+c=b+d via ratios of Beta integrals
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (Wallis-type products, E122 and others); Gauss 1812 for the Gamma form
ideas.where_published: E555 §17; Euler's papers on Wallis-type products/Beta integrals

ideas.what: Telescoping ratios 𝔅/𝔄, ℭ/𝔅, … expressing all cardinal coefficients via binomial coefficients (2n)_k/k!

missed.claim: The normalising Beta integral on this page is wrong: it should be 2B(n−ω, n+ω+1), not B(n−ω, n−ω). The resulting 'theorem' on the next page, ∫z^{−ω−1/2}(1−z)^{−ω−1/2}dz = (1+2ω)π/cos ωπ, is false, though it becomes true with the corrected Δ. I do not know whether the Opera omnia editors flagged this.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This corrects the historical record of Euler's interpolation results. Euler's own diagnosis (non-uniqueness of the interpolating curve) misidentifies the source of the discrepancy.

missed.claim: The formula is a Gamma-weighted cardinal series for odd functions on a shifted lattice. Euler's worry in the Scholion about whether the interpolant equals sin ωθ for non-lattice ω is precisely the uniqueness question later settled by growth conditions (Carlson's theorem, 1914; sampling theory). Euler's interest in interpolation uniqueness is known historically, so this is a mild connection.
missed.quote: Si fit x = nθ, (n+1)θ, … vt fiat y = p, q, r, …
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is an early explicit instance of a sampling/cardinal series with Beta-function normalisation, of minor historical interest.

deep.surprise_reason: The interpolation construction is a known Euler theme. The genuinely notable item is a concrete computational error in the Beta-integral normaliser, which makes the next page's evaluation false. Whether the editors noted this is unknown to me.
transcription_corrections: Parameters from §17: d should be 2n+1, not 1 (a+c=b+d requires d=2n+1).
𝔅/𝔄 should read (n−ω)(n+ω)/((n+1−ω)(n+1+ω))·(2+2n) = 2(n+1)(nn−ωω)/((n+1)²−ωω); this is consistent with the transcription.
The second and third lines of the product expansion have garbled denominators; correct factors are ((n+j)²−ω²)/((j−k)(2n+j+k)) for node n+k.
